rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is classified as late Makkan and reportedly followed Ṣād and preceded al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor:
A late Makkan sūrah, al-Aʿrāf was reportedly revealed afterṢād (
Sūrah 38) and just before al-Anʿām (
Sūrah 6).

rows.speaker: Al, IJ
rows.claim: Al and IJ consider verses 163–167 to have been revealed in Madinah.
rows.anchor:
Some,
however, have considered vv. 163–67 to have been revealed in
Madinah (Al, IJ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah warns of the grave consequences of rejecting God's signs and messengers, recalling prophets rejected by their peoples and the resulting suffering and destruction in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: the serious consequences of rejecting the signs and messengers of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its name from its reference to the Heights in verses 46 and 48.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Heights are variously identified as a high place in Paradise or as a place between Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor:
identified as a high place in Paradise or between Paradise and
Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immediate audience is idolatrous Makkans who refused to believe in Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor:
the idolatrous Makkans who refused to believe in
Muhammad’s prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah uses a subtler, less polemical argument than al-Anʿām, drawing on examples from earlier prophetic history.
rows.anchor:
a subtler and less
polemical approach, making its argument through reference to
examples from earlier prophetic history.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–10 remind listeners to follow divine guidance and warn generally of the consequences of failing to do so.
rows.anchor:
a reminder to follow Divine Guidance and a general
warning about the consequences of failing to do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–27 recount Adam's creation, temptation, and expulsion from the Garden.
rows.anchor:
the story of Adam’s creation, temptation, and exile from
the Garden.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account specifies that Adam and Eve sewed leaves from the Garden together to cover their newly discovered nakedness.
rows.anchor:
Adam
and Eve sewing together leaves from the Garden to cover their
newly discovered nakedness (v. 26)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative of Adam and Eve covering themselves leads into discussion of the virtue and limits of earthly adornment.
rows.anchor:
this narrative element is
then parlayed into a discussion of the virtue and limits of
earthly adornment in vv. 31–32.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 44–51 present a dialogue between the people of Paradise and the people of Hell in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: a dialogue between the people of Paradise and the people of Hell in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dialogue includes a somewhat cryptic reference to the inhabitants of the Heights.
rows.anchor: the somewhat cryptic mention of the inhabitants of the Heights

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A discourse on God's signs to humanity in verses 52–58 introduces extended accounts of earlier communities destroyed after rejecting their prophets.
rows.anchor: the various signs of God to humanity (vv. 52–58), which serves as an introduction to a lengthy segment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative recounts the destruction of Noah's people after their rejection of him.
rows.anchor: the peoples of the prophets Noah (vv. 59–64)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative recounts the destruction of Hūd's people after their rejection of him.
rows.anchor: the peoples of the prophets Noah (vv. 59–64), Hūd (vv. 65–72)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative recounts the destruction of Ṣāliḥ's people after their rejection of him.
rows.anchor: Ṣāliḥ (vv. 73–79)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative recounts the destruction of Lot's people after their rejection of him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative recounts the destruction of Shuʿayb's people after their rejection of him.
rows.anchor: Shuʿayb (vv. 85–93)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 104–126 give one of the Quran's most detailed accounts of Moses confronting Pharaoh and the sorcerers.
rows.anchor:
most
detailed accounts of Moses’ confrontation with Pharaoh and the sorcerers (vv. 104–26)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account describes punishments or plagues brought upon Egypt.
rows.anchor:
the various punishments or plagues
brought upon Egypt (vv. 130–36)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account describes Pharaoh and his hosts being destroyed and Israel delivered.
rows.anchor:
the eventual destruction of Pharaoh and his hosts and the deliverance of Israel (vv.
137–41)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses receives the Torah on the mountain.
rows.anchor:
Moses receiving the Torah on the mountain (vv.
142–47)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: During Moses' absence, the Israelites fashion a calf as an idol.
rows.anchor:
the Israelites fashioning a calf as an idol in his absence (vv.
148–54)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative proceeds to covenant making with Israel's elders.
rows.anchor:
the subsequent covenant making with the elders of Israel (vv.
155–56)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning Muhammad as the unlettered prophet, the surah says that the Torah and Gospel describe him.
rows.anchor: unlettered prophet”described in the Torah and Gospel (v. 157)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion returns to the Israelites' later disobedience and the future punishments they are said to suffer for it.
rows.anchor: the Israelites’ later disobedience and the future punishments they are said to suffer as a result (vv. 159–71)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 172 presents a universal, pretemporal covenant in which all human beings are bound to recognize God's Lordship; it grounds subsequent covenants between God and humanity mediated through prophets.
rows.anchor:
the universal, pretemporal covenant between God and all human beings
obligating them to recognize God’s Lordship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section again warns against denying God's signs and persisting in idolatry.
rows.anchor: repeats the warnings about denying the signs of God and persisting in idolatry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah closes with devotional practices, including invoking God's Names and listening to Quran recitation.
rows.anchor:
several verses dealing with pious and
devotional practices, including invoking the Names of God and
listening to the recitation of the Quran (vv. 180, 204–5).
